title: ⭐⭐ Practice: offers, one negative, and two things moving at once

questions.prompt: Two volunteers are at work in the reading room of a club in Gafsa. The first is going round the tables with a full tray, holding it out to one reader after another. The second has been sent along the corridor to find out whether there is still mint tea to be had at all. Which pair of sentences fits the two of them, in that order?

options.text: Can I get you any mint tea? Is there some mint tea left in the kitchen?
Can I get you some mint tea? Is there any mint tea left in the kitchen?
Can I get you some mint tea? Is there some mint tea left in the kitchen?
Can I get you any mint tea? Is there any mint tea left in the kitchen?

questions.explanation: "Can I get you some mint tea? Is there any mint tea left in the kitchen?" fits, and it fits twice over. A question that is really an offer or an invitation takes some: the volunteer with the tray is not asking whether tea exists, she is holding it out and expecting yes. The volunteer sent along the corridor is doing the opposite; she really is asking whether there is tea to be had at all, and a genuine question takes any. "Can I get you any mint tea? Is there some mint tea left in the kitchen?" turns each of them into the other: the offer stops being an offer and becomes an enquiry about whether tea can be found at all, while the enquiry stops enquiring and starts expecting yes. "Can I get you some mint tea? Is there some mint tea left in the kitchen?" gets the tray right and then keeps some in a question where nothing whatever is being offered. And "Can I get you any mint tea? Is there any mint tea left in the kitchen?" gets the kitchen right and hands the reader a question instead of a cup. Both words make a real English sentence here, and your book prints an offer both ways on the same page; what decides is what the speaker is doing while she speaks.

questions.prompt: Wassim is copying out, for the club's magazine, a note left by the man who kept the record shop of Le Kef. His copy reads: "We never sold no tickets for the summer concerts." The line carries one negative too many. Which correction keeps the meaning and is correct English?

options.text: We never sold any tickets for the summer concerts.
We didn't never sell any tickets for the summer concerts.
We sold not any tickets for the summer concerts.
We don't sell no tickets for the summer concerts.

questions.explanation: "We never sold any tickets for the summer concerts." repairs the line the right way: English marks a negative once, the negative stays in never, and the word after it takes the any- form. The other repair would have been to leave never out and put the negative in the word instead, we sold no tickets, but a clause may do one or the other, never both. "We didn't never sell any tickets for the summer concerts." puts the negative in twice again, once in didn't and once in never, so nothing has been repaired. "We sold not any tickets for the summer concerts." places not straight after a full verb, where English does not allow it; a full verb takes its negative through do. And "We don't sell no tickets for the summer concerts." keeps the double negative and, on top of that, moves a shop that has closed into the present.

questions.prompt: A librarian in Kairouan explains her opening hours like this: "When a reading room stays open late, more pupils come to it." She now wants to say the same thing as a rule, in a single sentence built on two comparatives. Which sentence says it?

options.text: The more late a reading room stays open, the more pupils come.
The latest a reading room stays open, the most pupils come to it.
Later a reading room stays open, more pupils come to it.
The later a reading room stays open, the more pupils come to it.

questions.explanation: "The later a reading room stays open, the more pupils come to it." is the rule she wants: two halves, each opening with the and each carrying a comparative, which is exactly how English ties two movements together. "The more late a reading room stays open, the more pupils come." marks the first comparative twice over, since late is short and builds its comparative with -er. "The latest a reading room stays open, the most pupils come to it." uses two superlatives, and a superlative ranks one item above all the others instead of linking two changes. And "Later a reading room stays open, more pupils come to it." drops both the, which are the two words that hold the halves together; without them the sentence falls into two loose pieces.

questions.prompt: A small record company in Sfax stopped answering a young group's calls and quietly took the group's songs off every list it publishes. Which verb of the lesson names what the company did to the group?

options.text: blamed
released
shunned
surpassed

questions.explanation: "shunned" is the verb: to shun somebody or something is to keep away from it on purpose, which is what a company does when it stops answering and removes the names from its lists. "blamed" would mean it said out loud that the group was responsible for something bad, and the point of the scene is that nothing was said at all. "released" is the opposite move: to release a record is to put it on sale. And "surpassed" means went beyond, did better than, so it needs a figure or a rival being beaten, not a group being avoided.

questions.prompt: Three of these four sentences use "some" or "any" as English requires. Which one does not?

options.text: The club wrote to the town hall, but it did not get some help with the rent.
Barely any light reached the top floor once the shutters had been closed.
I doubt whether the office keeps any records of the concerts of that year.
If the caretaker finds any of the missing programmes, he will put them aside.

questions.explanation: "The club wrote to the town hall, but it did not get some help with the rent." is the wrong one: it puts some after a negative verb, where English takes any, so the line should read it did not get any help with the rent. Each of the three others shows one of the places any belongs and uses it correctly. "Barely any light reached the top floor once the shutters had been closed." follows barely, which is almost a negative and pulls any after it exactly as not does; hardly and scarcely behave in the same way. "I doubt whether the office keeps any records of the concerts of that year." follows an expression of doubt. And "If the caretaker finds any of the missing programmes, he will put them aside." follows if, the fourth of the triggers. Polarity, not quantity, is what decides between the two words.

questions.prompt: The projector of a film club in Le Kef takes a bulb of an unusual size. Emna spent the afternoon on it: the two electrical shops of the town, then the market, then the school store. Back at the club she says: "I have not come across a single one ___." Which word fills the gap?

options.text: nowhere
somewhere
everywhere
anywhere

questions.explanation: "anywhere" is the word: the verb is already negative, have not, so the compound after it belongs to the any- series, and I have not come across a single one anywhere is the ordinary way of saying it. "nowhere" would mark the negative a second time: a clause puts its negative either in the verb or in the word, never in both, and here it is already in have not. "somewhere" belongs to affirmative statements and reverses her meaning entirely, since it would say she did come across one. And "everywhere" is not from these three series at all: I have not come across one everywhere would say there were places where she did come across one, which is the opposite of the afternoon she has just had.
